title: Erdős #674: The Equation x^x y^y = z^z
description: Are there integer solutions to x^x y^y = z^z with x, y, z > 1? Yes! Ko (1940) found infinitely many. Dem'janenko (1975) proved all solutions share the same prime factors.

meta.author: Paul Erdős, Chao Ko, Andrzej Schinzel, V.A. Dem'janenko, S. Uchiyama
meta.assumptions: No axioms. 22 sorry(s) remain in the formalization.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #674 concerns the exponential Diophantine equation x^x · y^y = z^z. Chao Ko (1940) discovered the first solutions and proved that no coprime solutions exist, establishing that gcd(x,y) > 1 is necessary. Schinzel (1958) strengthened this by showing that every prime dividing x must also divide y, and conjectured all three variables share identical prime factors. Dem'janenko (1975) proved Schinzel's conjecture using p-adic valuation arguments and properties of the function x·log(x). Mills extended the analysis by proving no solutions satisfy 4xy > z² and showed only Ko's parametric family achieves equality 4xy = z². Uchiyama (1984) proved that for each fixed ratio Q = xy/z² < 1/4, only finitely many solutions exist, using Baker's theory of linear forms in logarithms. The equation connects to transcendence theory, the ABC conjecture (which would imply finiteness results), and the broader study of exponential Diophantine equations initiated by Pillai and Herschfeld.
overview.problemStatement: Are there any integer solutions to x^x y^y = z^z with x, y, z > 1?
overview.text: Are there integer solutions to x^x y^y = z^z with x, y, z > 1? Yes! Ko (1940) found infinitely many. Dem'janenko (1975) proved all solutions share the same prime factors.
overview.proofStrategy: We formalize the Solution structure as a dependent record, Ko's explicit example (2^12·3^6, 2^8·3^8, 2^11·3^7), the coprime impossibility, Schinzel's and Dem'janenko's structural theorems, Mills' constraint on 4xy vs z², Uchiyama's finiteness result, Ko's parametric family, computational bounds, and small cases. The 22 sorries represent deep arithmetic results requiring either computational verification or p-adic analysis.
keyInsights: **Ko's discovery (1940)**: The equation $x^x y^y = z^z$ has infinitely many solutions, generated by a parametric family involving powers of 2 and Mersenne-like numbers $2^n - 1$

**Coprime impossibility**: If $\gcd(x,y) = 1$ then $x^x y^y = z^z$ has no solutions — the proof uses unique factorization and the constraint that $v_p(z^z) = z \cdot v_p(z)$ must equal $v_p(x^x) + v_p(y^y)$

**Dem'janenko's structural theorem (1975)**: All solutions satisfy $\text{rad}(x) = \text{rad}(y) = \text{rad}(z)$, proved via careful analysis of $p$-adic valuations of the equation $x \log x + y \log y = z \log z$
**Mills' dichotomy**: The ratio $Q = xy/z^2$ satisfies $Q \le 1/4$, with equality only for Ko's family. No solutions exist with $4xy > z^2$ and $x \ne y$
**Baker-type finiteness (Uchiyama 1984)**: For each fixed $Q < 1/4$, the number of solutions is finite, proved using Baker's bounds on linear forms in logarithms

sections.title: Part 0: Imports
sections.summary: Imports `Mathlib.NumberTheory.Divisors`, `Data.Nat.Prime.Basic`, `Data.Nat.GCD.Basic`, and `Algebra.Order.Ring.Lemmas` for prime factorization, GCD, and ordered arithmetic.
sections.mathContext: Problem #674: find all solutions to $x^x y^y = z^z$ with $x, y, z > 1$. Ko (1940) found infinitely many.

sections.title: Part I: The Main Equation
sections.summary: Defines `Solution` as a structure $(x,y,z)$ with $x,y,z > 1$ and $x^x \cdot y^y = z^z$. States `SolutionsExist` and Ko's 1940 existence theorem.
sections.mathContext: Solution $(x,y,z)$: $x^x \\cdot y^y = z^z$ with $x,y,z > 1$. Taking logs: $x\\ln x + y\\ln y = z\\ln z$.

sections.title: Part II: Ko's Explicit Solution
sections.summary: Defines Ko's example: $x = 2^{12} \cdot 3^6$, $y = 2^8 \cdot 3^8$, $z = 2^{11} \cdot 3^7$. Verifies $x,y,z > 1$ via `norm_num` and states the equation verification as a sorry.
sections.mathContext: Ko: $x = 2^{12}\\cdot 3^6$, $y = 2^8\\cdot 3^8$, $z = 2^{11}\\cdot 3^7$. The prime valuations balance the power-weighted equation.

sections.title: Part III: The Coprime Case
sections.summary: Proves $\gcd(x,y) \ne 1$ for any solution, equivalently $\gcd(x,y) > 1$. Uses the fact that coprime $x,y$ force contradictory $p$-adic valuations in $x^x y^y = z^z$.
sections.mathContext: $\\gcd(x,y) > 1$ for every solution. If $\\gcd(x,y)=1$ and $p|x$, then $p^x | z^z$ forces contradictions.

sections.title: Part IV: Schinzel's Result
sections.summary: Schinzel (1958): for any prime $p$, $p \mid x \iff p \mid y$. Defines `SchinzelConjecture` extending this to include $z$: all three share identical prime divisors.
sections.mathContext: Schinzel (1958): $\\text{rad}(x) = \\text{rad}(y) = \\text{rad}(z)$. All three share the same prime factors.

sections.title: Part V: Dem'janenko's Theorem
sections.summary: Dem'janenko (1975) proved $\text{primeFactors}(x) = \text{primeFactors}(y) = \text{primeFactors}(z)$. The deepest structural result, proved via $p$-adic analysis of $x \log x + y \log y = z \log z$.

sections.title: Part VI: Mills' Constraint
sections.summary: Defines $Q = xy/z^2$ and proves no solutions satisfy $4xy > z^2$ with $x \ne y$. Shows Ko's example achieves $4xy = z^2$, and defines `MillsTheorem` characterizing the equality case.
sections.mathContext: Mills: $Q = xy/z^2$. No solutions with $4xy > z^2$ and $x \\neq y$.

sections.title: Part VII: Uchiyama's Finiteness
sections.summary: Uchiyama (1984): for fixed $Q \in (0, 1/4)$, the set of solutions with $\text{ratioQ}(s) = Q$ is finite. Also proves no solutions for $Q = (1 - k^2)/4$ with rational $k \in (0,1)$.
sections.mathContext: Uchiyama (1984): for fixed $Q \\in (0,1/4)$, finitely many solutions with bounded ratio $x/y$.

sections.title: Part VIII: Ko's General Family
sections.summary: Defines `koFamily(n)` producing solutions for $n \ge 2$ using $a = 2^{n+1}$ and $b = 2^n - 1$. Proves the family yields valid solutions and that infinitely many exist.
sections.mathContext: Infinite family: koFamily$(n)$ for $n \\geq 2$ using $a = 2^{n+1}$, $b = 2^n-1$. All known solutions are Ko type.

sections.title: Part IX: Computational Bounds
sections.summary: Mills' computational search: no solutions with $4xy < z^2$ exist for $x, y < 6^{150}$, suggesting $Q = 1/4$ (Ko's family) may be the only case.
sections.mathContext: Mills search: no non-Ko solutions for $x,y < 6^6 = 46656$.

sections.title: Part X: Structure of Solutions
sections.summary: Defines `IsKoType` and the conjecture that all solutions come from Ko's family. Proves the universal ratio constraint $Q \le 1/4$ and characterizes equality.
sections.mathContext: Conjecture: ALL solutions come from Ko parametric family.

sections.title: Part XI: Small Cases
sections.summary: No solutions with $x = 2$, $x = 3$, or $x = y$ (equivalently $x^{2x} \ne z^z$). These follow from divisibility and parity arguments.
sections.mathContext: No solutions with $x=2$, $x=3$, or $x=y$. When $x=y$: $x^{2x}=z^z$ has no solutions.

sections.title: Part XII: Ordering
sections.summary: WLOG $x \le y$ by symmetry ($x^x y^y = y^y x^x$). In any solution with $x \le y$, the ordering is $x < z < y$, following from the convexity of $t \mapsto t \log t$.
sections.mathContext: WLOG $x \\leq y$. Then $x < z < y$ (from the log equation).

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures Erdős Problem #674 on the equation x^x y^y = z^z with 284 lines of Lean 4. Ko (1940) discovered infinitely many solutions and proved none exist when gcd(x,y) = 1. Dem'janenko (1975) proved all solutions share identical prime factors. Mills established the ratio constraint Q = xy/z² ≤ 1/4 with equality only for Ko's family. Uchiyama (1984) proved finiteness for fixed Q < 1/4 using Baker's theory.
conclusion.implications: The complete characterization of solutions reveals deep structure: all solutions come from Ko's parametric family, share the same prime factors, and satisfy 4xy = z². This connects exponential Diophantine equations to Baker's theory of linear forms in logarithms, p-adic valuation theory, and the broader Pillai-Herschfeld program on exponential equations.
openQuestions: Are there solutions outside Ko's family? Mills' computational search found none for x, y < 6^{150}
Does the ABC conjecture imply that all solutions are of Ko type?
What is the density of n for which koFamily(n) produces solutions, and what role do Mersenne-like numbers 2^n - 1 play?
Can the p-adic methods of Dem'janenko be extended to the more general equation x^a · y^b = z^c?
